extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in Frankie Boyle and contemporary British comedy
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia biography page summarising Frankie Boyle's life, career, controversies, and public reception; includes editorial tags and sourced excerpts about broadcasting/regulatory responses to his humour. Useful for readers seeking an overview of the comedian and incidents that generated complaints or regulatory action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biography of living person sourcing requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: "This section of a biography of a living person needs additional citations for verification. Please help by adding reliable sources. Contentious material about living persons that is unsourced or poorly sourced must be removed immediately from the article and its talk page, especially if potentially libelous."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page-level Wikipedia policy: add reliable sources for contentious claims about living people; remove unsourced or poorly sourced contentious material immediately (particularly if potentially libelous).

rubrics_metrics.name: BBC assessment of offensive material
rubrics_metrics.description: "The BBC ruled that the jokes were indeed 'humiliating' and 'risked offending the audience', while also calling Boyle 'a brilliant member of the team'."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcasting organisations (here, the BBC) may evaluate humour against editorial standards and describe content using terms like 'humiliating' or 'risked offending the audience', leading to formal rebukes or apologies even when the performer is still recognised for talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ofcom broadcasting rules and investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: "Ofcom confirmed that Price issued a complaint and accordingly launched an investigation into the programme." and "Ofcom ruled Channel 4 had breached broadcasting rules by transmitting the material in question but did not require the network to broadcast an apology saying that it was an 'erroneous decision on a matter of editorial judgment on the broadcaster's part'."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory body Ofcom can investigate complaints about broadcast content and rule that a broadcaster breached rules; outcomes can include findings against broadcasters but do not always require on-air apologies — decisions may frame issues as editorial judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public norm: children and disabled people should be off-limits
rubrics_metrics.description: "Children, especially a disabled youngster, should be off-limits." (statement by Peter Andre's representative regarding a joke about Katie Price's disabled son)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representatives, charities, and members of the public may assert normative limits on comedic targets (e.g., children or disabled people), and breaching those norms often provokes strong complaints, reputational harm, and formal investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcasters may cut or omit material judged distasteful
rubrics_metrics.description: "This was deemed so distasteful that his entire six-minute performance was cut out of the broadcast version of the 3.5-hour show."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if material is performed live, broadcasters exercise editorial control and may remove segments from televised/broadcast versions when deemed distasteful or inappropriate for the broadcast audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation/libel consequences for published allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: "In July 2011, the Daily Mirror published an article strongly criticising Boyle which alleged he had been forced to quit Mock the Week and described him as a 'racist comedian'. Boyle, in response, sued the Mirror for libel. In October 2012, a jury found in his favour, ordering the Mirror to pay him £54,650 in damages..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media outlets publishing allegations about individuals can face libel actions; defamatory or false assertions in press coverage can result in damages awarded and reputational/legal consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topics that frequently provoke complaints and regulatory attention
rubrics_metrics.description: The article documents multiple controversy examples (Rebecca Adlington remarks; impersonation of the Queen described as 'sexist and ageist'; jokes about Down's syndrome; Palestinian/Israel jokes; jokes about Katie Price's disabled son; rape jokes about public figures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject matter touching on disability, children, rape/sexual violence, protected groups, national/religious identities, and prominent public figures repeatedly attracts complaints, regulatory scrutiny, apologies or removals — these topic areas are recurrent triggers for controversy in broadcast and public contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial judgement vs. public/regulatory standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples across the page show tension between a comedian's editorial/creative choices and broadcasters' or regulators' responses (e.g., BBC/Channel 4 decisions, Ofcom rulings, producers editing material).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is an ongoing balance between editorial freedom (creative/performer's intent) and external standards (public norms, broadcaster policies, regulator rules); outcomes depend on institutional judgments, complaints, and legal/regulatory frameworks.
